The browser still exits, so the "Profile Missing" popup is still there. I couldn't find the failing step in this build, and I'm stopping rather than guessing further.

**What I found**
- The popup comes from `ProfileMissingDialog` in `toolkit/xre/nsAppRunner.cpp`. It fires in two cases: `nsToolkitProfileService::Init()` fails, or `SelectProfile()` fails. Both return the same dialog, so the popup alone doesn't tell them apart.
- `Init()` depends on the app-data directory lookup and reading `profiles.ini`. Neither was obviously broken. `~/Library/Application Support/Mozilla/` has only a `Firefox.synapse-workaround-backup` folder and a `NativeMessagingHosts` folder, so there's no live profile to conflict with.
- These failures use `NS_WARNING` and `NS_ERROR`, which print nothing in an optimized build. That's why `MOZ_LOG` and stderr showed nothing useful. Finding the exact step needs a debug build or a build with logging enabled.

**Fixed so far**
- The GPU helper name mismatch. [config/mozconfig.in](config/mozconfig.in) now uses `--disable-artifact-builds`, and the compiled binary contains `Synapse GPU Helper`.
- Signing. The packaged bundle had 7,881 symlinks into the source and build trees, which `codesign` rejects. I replaced them with real copies in the `dist` output, and `codesign --verify` passes. This was a one-off fix in build output. The `tools/synapse-macos.sh` script still doesn't sign or dereference symlinks, so a fresh package will hit the same problem.

**Not fixed**
- The browser still exits about a minute after launch, and the "Profile Missing" dialog is what it reaches. I haven't identified the cause.

**Next step:** I'd rebuild with logging enabled, either a debug build or `--enable-logging`, then rerun to see which `Init()` or `SelectProfile()` step fails. That is a large rebuild. Alternatively, I could make `tools/synapse-macos.sh` dereference symlinks and sign the bundle so packaging is repeatable. Tell me which you'd like.

`XREMain::XRE_mainStartup` (`toolkit/xre/nsAppRunner.cpp`) has two paths into
`ProfileMissingDialog`:

```cpp

if (!mProfileSvc) {                 // (A) nsToolkitProfileService::Init() failed
  ProfileMissingDialog(mNativeApp);
  return 1;
}
...
rv = SelectProfile(mProfileSvc, ...);
if (NS_FAILED(rv)) {                // (B) SelectProfile failed
  ProfileMissingDialog(mNativeApp);
  return 1;

It's fixed and verified. Here's the summary.

## Root cause

Synapse was writing its profile into **Firefox's** application-data directory. macOS refuses to create that path for this app:

- `mkdir "~/Library/Application Support/Firefox"` → **Operation not permitted**, while `Synapse`, `TestApp`, `Firefox2` and even `Mozilla/Firefox` all succeed.
- `nsToolkitProfileService::Init()` → `GetUserAppDataDirectory()` → `EnsureDirectoryExists()` returned `0x80520015` (`NS_ERROR_FILE_ACCESS_DENIED`), so `Init()` aborted and `XRE_mainStartup` fell through to the "Profile Missing" alert.
- Proof it was only the destination: with `MOZ_APP_DATA=/tmp/...` the browser initialised fully (profiles.ini, a profile, profile groups) and ran.

Why the earlier `application.ini` edits did nothing: the ini is compiled into the binary as `sAppData` (`browser/app/ApplicationData.cpp`), so the on-disk copy is ignored, and each build regenerates it anyway. The name comes from `Name=@MOZ_APP_BASENAME@` in `build/application.ini.in`.

## The fix

One option in [config/mozconfig.in](config/mozconfig.in) — `ac_add_options --with-app-basename=Synapse` — which upstream documents as controlling `application.ini`'s `Name` and therefore the profile location. This is the same shape of rebrand LibreWolf does: its own profile directory, not Firefox's.

**Verified after a clean rebuild (39 min):** `MOZ_APP_BASENAME = Synapse`, `Name=Synapse`, `~/Library/Application Support/Synapse` created with a real `profiles.ini`, headless alive at 18 s with zero "profile folder" errors, GUI alive at 22 s with no alert. All temporary `SYNDIAG` instrumentation has been reverted; the Firefox tree is back to just your pre-existing overlay changes.

Side effect worth knowing: the basename also derives `MOZ_APP_NAME`, so the executable is now `Contents/MacOS/synapse` (not `firefox`), and `dist/bin` still holds a stale `firefox` from the previous build.

## Handoff

[docs/HANDOFF-codex.md](docs/HANDOFF-codex.md) covers the symptom, the full evidence table, why each earlier hypothesis was wrong, the fix, the verification log, and the remaining gaps: packaging still isn't reproducible (7,881 symlinks break `codesign`, and `tools/synapse-macos.sh` doesn't dereference or sign), the bundle holds real copies so `mach build` doesn't update it, and there's a separate `console.error: Policies:` at startup worth chasing.

Nothing is committed — `config/mozconfig.in` and the new handoff are uncommitted in the repo, and `.DS_Store` is an unrelated modification.

+# Handoff: Synapse macOS build and the "Profile Missing" startup failure
+
+Last updated: 2026-10-27. Author: Buffy (Freebuff). Successor: Codex.
+
+## TL;DR
+
+**Root cause found and fixed.** Synapse was writing its profile into *Firefox's*
+application-data directory. macOS refuses to create that path for this app
+(`NS_ERROR_FILE_ACCESS_DENIED`), so `nsToolkitProfileService::Init()` aborted, and
+`XRE_mainStartup` fell through to the "Profile Missing" alert.
+
+The fix is one configure option in `config/mozconfig.in`:
+
+```sh
+ac_add_options --with-app-basename=Synapse
+```
+
+**Rebuilt and verified** on 2026-10-27 (see "Verification log"): headless and GUI runs
+both start, stay up, and create `~/Library/Application Support/Synapse` with a real
+`profiles.ini`. The "Profile Missing" alert is gone.
+
+Independent corroboration: LibreWolf, a comparable full rebrand, likewise uses its own
+profile directory instead of Firefox's — which is exactly the property this change
+restores.
+
+## Symptom
+
+Launching `dist/Synapse.app` (or `mach run`) showed the macOS **"Profile Missing"**
+alert, the process exited 1 within seconds, no profile was ever created, and
+`~/Library/Application Support/Firefox` never appeared. Headless runs printed
+`Could not find profile folder.` instead of the alert.
+
+## Root cause, with evidence
+
+Chain:
+
+1. `XREMain::XRE_mainStartup` (`toolkit/xre/nsAppRunner.cpp`) calls
+   `NS_GetToolkitProfileService()`.
+2. That calls `nsToolkitProfileService::Init()`
+   (`toolkit/profile/nsToolkitProfileService.cpp`), whose first real step is
+   `nsXREDirProvider::GetUserAppDataDirectory()`.
+3. `GetUserDataDirectory()` (`toolkit/xre/nsXREDirProvider.cpp`) resolves
+   `~/Library/Application Support/<gAppData->name>` and calls
+   `EnsureDirectoryExists()`, i.e. `nsIFile::Create()`.
+4. `Create()` fails with **EPERM**, surfaced as `0x80520015`.
+   `NS_ENSURE_SUCCESS` returns it, `Init()` fails,
+   `NS_GetToolkitProfileService()` returns null, and the alert is shown.
+5. Because the app-data dir is created *before* any profile handling, every launch
+   form fails identically: `-profile <dir>`, `-P name`, `-CreateProfile`,
+   `-profilemanager`, a fresh `HOME`, headless or GUI.
+
+`0x80520015` is `NS_ERROR_FILE_ACCESS_DENIED`
+(`FAILURE(21)` in `xpcom/base/ErrorList.py`).
+
+Measured, on this machine (`MAC16,12`, macOS 27.2):
+
+| Test | Result |
+| --- | --- |
+| `mkdir ~/Library/Application Support/Firefox` | **Operation not permitted** |
+| same, lowercase `firefox` | denied (case-insensitive volume) |
+| `mkdir ~/Library/Application Support/Firefox2` | OK |
+| `mkdir ~/Library/Application Support/Synapse` | OK |
+| `mkdir ~/Library/Application Support/Mozilla/Firefox` | OK |
+| `mkdir ~/Library/Application Support/TestApp` | OK |
+| app with `MOZ_APP_DATA=~/Library/Application Support/SynTest4` | `rv=0`, browser **runs** |
+| app with `MOZ_APP_DATA=~/Library/Application Support/Firefox` | `rv=0x80520015` |
+
+So the block is on that one literal path — macOS is protecting the data directory it
+associates with Firefox and denying it to this app. Everything else on the volume is
+writable by the same process, including sibling names in the same directory.
+
+With `MOZ_APP_DATA=/tmp/synad/app` (a throwaway dir) the browser initialised fully:
+`installs.ini`, `profiles.ini`, `Profiles/<id>.default-default`, `Profiles/<id>.default`,
+`Profile Groups/`, `Crash Reports/` were all created, `Init()` returned `rv=0` at every
+step, and the process stayed alive for 40 s headless and 20 s in GUI mode. **The
+browser itself is fine; only the destination directory is refused.**
+
+### Why editing `application.ini` did nothing
+
+`application.ini` is compiled into the binary as `sAppData`
+(`browser/app/ApplicationData.cpp` → `kStaticAppData`, used by
+`browser/app/nsBrowserApp.cpp` when no `-app` flag is given). The copy on disk under
+`Contents/Resources/` is not what supplies the name at runtime, so editing
+`Name=` there (tried with `Synapse` and `SynProbe`) changed nothing — the resolved
+path stayed `.../Firefox`. Rebuilding also regenerates that file from the template,
+discarding such edits.
+
+The value comes from `build/application.ini.in`:
+
+```
+Name=@MOZ_APP_BASENAME@
+```
+
+and `MOZ_APP_BASENAME` is configured by `--with-app-basename`
+(`build/moz.configure/init.configure`, option at ~line 1263). Its upstream help text
+states it is "Used for application.ini's Name field, which controls profile location".
+On macOS the vendor is ignored and only the app name is appended
+(`nsXREDirProvider.cpp`, `AppendProfilePath`).
+
+## The fix
+
+`config/mozconfig.in`:
+
+```sh
+ac_add_options --with-app-basename=Synapse
+```
+
+This is a full-rebrand knob (upstream cites Iceweasel), which is the right shape for
+this product: Synapse should not share Firefox's application-data directory, which on
+a machine with a real Firefox install is also a collision waiting to happen.
+
+**Side effect to expect:** `MOZ_APP_NAME` defaults to the lowercase form of the
+basename, so after reconfiguring this build reports
+`MOZ_APP_BASENAME = Synapse` / `MOZ_APP_NAME = synapse`
+(`.synapse-build/obj-synapse/config/autoconf.mk`, confirmed). The executable is
+therefore `Synapse.app/Contents/MacOS/synapse`, not `.../firefox`, and anything that
+hard-codes the old binary name (scripts, notes, aliases) needs updating. The bundle id
+`org.synapse.browser` is unaffected. If the rename is not wanted, the alternative is
+to keep the basename and set the profile location through some other supported knob —
+but note the compile-time app data name is what decides the directory, so a runtime
+`application.ini` edit cannot do it.
+
+After a successful build, app data lives in `~/Library/Application Support/Synapse`,
+which this machine permits.
+

+

Synapse Browser Feature Requirements
Development handoff and release checklist
October 27 2026
Synapse should be a dependable everyday browser with clear privacy controls, isolated identities, Firefox extension compatibility, and reliable macOS and Windows releases. Build the everyday experience first, and enable advanced network modes only when their protections are verified end to end.
How to use this document
This is the recommended product backlog. Each requirement has an identifier, a priority, and an observable completion condition. Ask the implementation team to mark each item Verified, Partial, Missing, or Deferred and attach the build version and evidence. Inherited Firefox features still need testing in the shipped Synapse application.
The browser is now running according to the latest project update. Feature completion remains to be checked against FreBuff’s handoff and the actual build. This checklist does not assume that an earlier blocker is still present or that a privacy policy contract proves network enforcement.
Priority definitions
P0 means required before a public everyday release. Failures can affect security, data, updates, or basic browsing.
P1 means required for the complete Synapse product experience. Deliver after P0 is stable, or alongside it when dependencies allow.
P2 means a later enhancement. These items should not delay a stable, secure first release.
Gate means mandatory before enabling or advertising the associated capability, even when that capability is scheduled after the first release.
Delivery order
First stabilize browsing, profiles, security defaults, recovery, packaging, and updates. Next finish the Synapse interface, identity workflows, and extensions. Then enable Tor and I2P independently after their gates pass. Keep Blackout unavailable until its stronger isolation and cleanup requirements pass. Add optional sync and productivity features afterward.
Everyday browsing
Requirements and completion checks

SYN 002  P0  Tabs and windows. Create, close, reopen, duplicate, pin, move, reorder, detach, and mute tabs. Multiple windows and modifier clicks behave consistently; closing a busy window protects against accidental loss.

SYN 006  P0  Downloads. Show progress, cancel, retry, reveal files, and choose destinations. Handle duplicate names and interrupted downloads safely; warn before opening executable or externally handled content.

That means I2P should have a clear entry point, visible route and connection status, and its own persistent profile for each identity, kept separate from that identity’s regular browsing profile. If the I2P router or proxy is unavailable, Synapse must block I2P browsing rather than silently fall back to a direct connection. The current project has a Windows I2P+ development path, but it is still a separate launcher flow; bringing it into the main browser experience is part of the product goal.

I’ll also keep the distinction clear from Tor: I2P destinations and optional clearnet outproxy traffic have different routing semantics, so the UI should say what is actually routed rather than imply all I2P-mode traffic is `.i2p`-only.

Progress note:
It's fixed and verified. Here's the summary.

## Root cause

Synapse was writing its profile into **Firefox's** application-data directory. macOS refuses to create that path for this app:

- `mkdir "~/Library/Application Support/Firefox"` → **Operation not permitted**, while `Synapse`, `TestApp`, `Firefox2` and even `Mozilla/Firefox` all succeed.
- `nsToolkitProfileService::Init()` → `GetUserAppDataDirectory()` → `EnsureDirectoryExists()` returned `0x80520015` (`NS_ERROR_FILE_ACCESS_DENIED`), so `Init()` aborted and `XRE_mainStartup` fell through to the "Profile Missing" alert.
- Proof it was only the destination: with `MOZ_APP_DATA=/tmp/...` the browser initialised fully (profiles.ini, a profile, profile groups) and ran.

Why the earlier `application.ini` edits did nothing: the ini is compiled into the binary as `sAppData` (`browser/app/ApplicationData.cpp`), so the on-disk copy is ignored, and each build regenerates it anyway. The name comes from `Name=@MOZ_APP_BASENAME@` in `build/application.ini.in`.

## The fix

One option in [config/mozconfig.in](config/mozconfig.in) — `ac_add_options --with-app-basename=Synapse` — which upstream documents as controlling `application.ini`'s `Name` and therefore the profile location. This is the same shape of rebrand LibreWolf does: its own profile directory, not Firefox's.

**Verified after a clean rebuild (39 min):** `MOZ_APP_BASENAME = Synapse`, `Name=Synapse`, `~/Library/Application Support/Synapse` created with a real `profiles.ini`, headless alive at 18 s with zero "profile folder" errors, GUI alive at 22 s with no alert. All temporary `SYNDIAG` instrumentation has been reverted; the Firefox tree is back to just your pre-existing overlay changes.

Side effect worth knowing: the basename also derives `MOZ_APP_NAME`, so the executable is now `Contents/MacOS/synapse` (not `firefox`), and `dist/bin` still holds a stale `firefox` from the previous build.

## Handoff

[docs/HANDOFF-codex.md](docs/HANDOFF-codex.md) covers the symptom, the full evidence table, why each earlier hypothesis was wrong, the fix, the verification log, and the remaining gaps: packaging still isn't reproducible (7,881 symlinks break `codesign`, and `tools/synapse-macos.sh` doesn't dereference or sign), the bundle holds real copies so `mach build` doesn't update it, and there's a separate `console.error: Policies:` at startup worth chasing.

Nothing is committed — `config/mozconfig.in` and the new handoff are uncommitted in the repo, and `.DS_Store` is an unrelated modification.

Since the policies errors are the next visible wart at startup, that's the natural place to keep going — I'd trace whether the generated `distribution/policies.json` is malformed or a policy key is unsupported in this Gecko version.

**Users should opt in manually.** I found no I2P+ or upstream I2P documentation describing a supported way for an installer, router package, or third party to silently preconfigure `http://skank.i2p/hosts.txt` as a subscription. The documented I2P+ instructions present it as an optional, user-initiated choice.

### Documented I2P+ procedure and endpoints

The I2P+ FAQ says users who want the I2P+ console’s linked I2P domains to resolve without jump links can add this subscription in their own address book:

`http://skank.i2p/hosts.txt`

The FAQ links the subscription-management page at:

`http://127.0.0.1:7657/susidns/subscriptions`

It also documents an alternative: import the I2P+ `hosts.txt` file through SusiDNS’s Import function, with the SusiDNS link pointing to:

`http://127.0.0.1:7657/dns`

These are local Router Console endpoints; the documented links use the default local address and port. The I2P+ homepage independently describes adding the subscription or using the import option, though it does not spell out the local paths.

### What upstream I2P docs establish

The official I2P naming/address-book docs explain that SusiDNS is the web front end for address-book configuration. They say the default subscription is the I2P project’s list, and that **users must configure additional subscriptions locally**, either through `subscriptions.txt` or SusiDNS.

Those docs also warn that subscribing to another party’s `hosts.txt` involves trust: a list operator could potentially supply a conflicting hostname entry. The docs say providers may have different listing policies and that presence on a list does not imply endorsement.

### Conclusion on preconfiguration

The sources support **manual opt-in**, not silent preconfiguration. The upstream docs’ mention of `subscriptions.txt` identifies a local configuration route; it is not, in the material reviewed, a recommendation or procedure for third parties to preseed users’ subscription lists. The I2P+ docs likewise describe a user adding the subscription or importing the file. So I would not characterize automatic preconfiguration as documented or supported; users should decide whether to add the feed.

Import is a documented alternative to subscribing, but the pages reviewed do not specify whether an import is periodically refreshed. Treat it as the documented import option, not as equivalent to a recurring subscription.

+  local profile="$1"
+  local target="$profile/user.js"
+  local staged
+  if [[ -e "$target" ]] && ! grep -Fq '// Generated by Synapse. Dedicated I2P+ profile.' "$target"; then

+  fi
+  if [[ -e "$target" ]]; then
+    local existing staged_content
+    existing="$(cat "$target")"
+    staged="$(mktemp "$profile/.user.js.XXXXXX")"
+    chmod 600 "$staged"
+    write_i2p_prefs_to "$staged"
+    staged_content="$(cat "$staged")"

+  chmod 600 "$staged"

+  mv -f "$staged" "$target"

Findings

**I2P+ is a Java-based fork of the I2P router, not a browser library or a Java-free embedded router.** Its official site describes it as an enhanced Java I2P platform, and the I2P project’s alternative-clients documentation says I2P+ requires a Java environment. The I2P project identifies I2P+ as a community-maintained fork, distinct from its own official Java I2P release.  
Sources: [I2P+ home](https://i2pplus.github.io/); [I2P project: Alternative I2P Clients](https://i2p.net/en/docs/overview/alternative-clients/).

### Installers and runtime

- **I2P+ publishes a universal installer for Windows, Linux, BSD, and macOS**, plus update ZIPs. Its download page says downloads are compatible with **Java 8 or later** unless otherwise stated. For non-Windows systems, the `.exe` is a Windows-specific wrapper around the JAR; the documented command is `java -jar ./i2pinstall.exe`.  
  Sources: [I2P+ Download](https://i2pplus.github.io/download.html); [I2P+ Installation Guide](https://i2pplus.github.io/installation.html).
- The installation instructions require Java to run the installer and router. I found **no indication in I2P+’s official download or installation pages that its universal installer bundles a Java runtime**. Plan to provide a compatible Java runtime yourself or require one to be installed; Java licensing and redistribution obligations are separate from I2P+’s license.
- I2P+ does document Windows and macOS installation paths, but its published package is presented as a universal installer—not as a native macOS `.pkg`/`.dmg` or Windows `.msi` package. The source repository documents build targets for OS-specific installers and ZIPs; those build instructions are not themselves evidence of signed, supported native packages.  
  Sources: [I2P+ Download](https://i2pplus.github.io/download.html); [I2P+ repository](https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/).
- **Don’t assume the Windows `.exe` installer works with every Java distribution.** I2P+’s repository warns that with Java newer than 1.8 or alternative distributions, the installer executable may report Java missing or corrupt; its workaround is extracting `install.jar` from the `.exe` and running it with `java -jar install.jar`.  
  Source: [I2P+ repository](https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/).
- The upstream I2P project’s download page advertises some Easy Installer builds that bundle Java, but this is **upstream I2P guidance, not an I2P+ package**. The download page could not be fetched during research, so I could not verify its current platform/version details directly.  
  URL: [I2P downloads](https://geti2p.net/en/download).

### Redistribution and bundling

I2P+ states that it is licensed under the **GNU Affero General Public License version 3 or later**, and says it may be redistributed and modified under that license. Its repository makes source available and provides a separate inventory of component licenses.  
Sources: [I2P+ repository](https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/); [I2P+ license and component notices](https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/blob/master/docs/LICENSES.md).

**In short: redistribution is allowed, but it is conditional.** When conveying I2P+ to users, follow the AGPL’s applicable requirements for license and copyright notices, source availability, and modified versions. The AGPL is not a blanket permission to fold I2P+ into a proprietary combined work under closed terms. Whether a desktop browser and a separately installed or separately launched router constitute an independent aggregate, or a combined work, depends on how they are integrated; the project’s license page does not resolve that product-specific question. Review the AGPL and get legal advice for a commercial bundling design. Also check the listed licenses for third-party components and any Java runtime you bundle.  
Sources: [I2P+ license and component notices](https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/blob/master/docs/LICENSES.md); [GNU AGPL v3](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.en.html).

### Packaging and support caveats

- I2P+ has its **own support channels** and its own release/update path. Its site directs users to I2P-network IRC `#saltR` or Libera IRC `#i2p+`; the repository also points to its issue tracker. Don’t imply that an I2P+ bundle is supported by the upstream I2P project.  
  Sources: [I2P+ home](https://i2pplus.github.io/); [I2P+ repository](https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/).
- The documented installer installs a router, not just browser-side connectivity. I2P+ documents a Windows service, for which service control may require administrator privileges; it also documents separate application and settings directories. Treat router lifecycle, persistence, upgrades, and user data as part of the packaging/integration work.  
  Source: [I2P+ Installation Guide](https://i2pplus.github.io/installation.html).
- The project’s update guidance describes copying `i2pupdate.zip` into an existing installation and restarting the router. Its FAQ warns users moving from the upstream Easy Installer to uninstall it and remove or rename the existing `%appdata%\i2p` folder; this is a migration caveat worth handling carefully in an app installer or upgrade flow. The FAQ page presents an older version in its page title, so rely on the current download page for release availability.  
  Sources: [I2P+ FAQ](https://i2pplus.github.io/faq.html); [I2P+ Download](https://i2pplus.github.io/download.html).

**Practical takeaway:** I2P+ appears redistributable under AGPL terms, but its official packaging guidance is for a Java-dependent router installation, not a turnkey browser-app bundle. Before shipping, decide whether Java is a prerequisite or bundled component; satisfy I2P+ and component licensing/source obligations; test the Windows installer workaround; and define who manages the router service, updates, and user data."}]}

Yes—**I2P+ can be redistributed**, so bundling it is a viable direction. Its project says it’s licensed under **AGPL-3.0-or-later**; shipping it means including the required notices and license, and making the corresponding source available for the exact version you distribute, including any changes. How it should be licensed alongside Synapse depends on how the two programs are packaged and connected, so that part deserves a legal review before release.

There’s also a runtime issue: I2P+ is a Java router, and its installer documentation calls for Java 8 or later. Bundling Java too is possible only after choosing a runtime distribution and checking its redistribution terms. I2P+’s published installer is not a turnkey browser bundle.

**My recommendation:** make I2P+ an optional, Synapse-managed component, with a clear install/skip choice and controls for starting and updating the router. That avoids requiring users to set it up separately, while keeping it distinct from the browser. The macOS path we have today still expects an already-running router; it doesn’t install or bundle I2P+.

Sources: [I2P+ downloads](https://i2pplus.github.io/download.html), [I2P+ installation guide](https://i2pplus.github.io/installation.html), [I2P+ license and component notices](https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/blob/master/docs/LICENSES.md), [GNU AGPLv3](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.en.html).

A useful next step would be to outline the optional bundled-router install and update flow.

**Yes: a normal I2P+ router process can be started and stopped by the logged-in macOS user; administrator privileges are not inherently required.** The documented cross-platform launcher is `i2prouter`, not just the Mac “Start I2P Router” app:

```sh
cd /Applications/i2p
sh i2prouter start       # start
sh i2prouter graceful    # graceful shutdown
sh i2prouter stop        # immediate stop
sh i2prouter status      # report status
```

The I2P+ headless guide explicitly documents `sh i2prouter start`, graceful and immediate stop, and says the start command applies to “Linux, BSD, Mac.” The I2P+ install guide lists Apple’s default non-repository application directory as `/Applications/i2p/`. The source’s Unix `i2prouter` script contains macOS-specific behavior, including detection of Darwin and macOS configuration paths.

**Status caveat:** The script is the relevant management interface, but the documentation is uneven: the headless guide spells out start and stop, while the general install guide’s explicit `status` command is in the *Linux system-service* section. I found no macOS-specific docs page listing a separate status command. So `sh i2prouter status` is the script-level status method; the docs do not present it as a distinct macOS/launchd status procedure.

## User process versus launchd service

These are separate modes:

- **User-launched router:** Run the script as the account that owns the installation/configuration. The ordinary start/stop commands do not install or manage a system service, and the script has a per-user configuration directory. Thus there is no inherent need for `sudo` to operate the user’s router. The account does need permission to read/execute the app files and write its configuration/log files.
- **System launchd service:** I2P+ also ships macOS service-install and service-uninstall scripts. The installer writes a plist to `/Library/LaunchDaemons/net.i2p.router.plist`, invokes `sudo`, sets ownership to `root:wheel`, and loads it with `launchctl`. Its uninstall script likewise uses `sudo`. **Installing or removing this system service requires administrator privileges**; that is different from starting/stopping a user-owned router process. The service plist runs the router as the named user, starts at load, and is configured to keep it alive.

The macOS service installer explicitly requests a password for “sudo privileges.” Do not interpret that as meaning every router start/stop requires admin rights: it applies to this system-wide launchd setup. I2P+’s general Linux service commands likewise use `sudo`, but those Linux instructions are not macOS launchd instructions.

## Paths and practical caveats

- **Application files:** `/Applications/i2p/` is the published default for a non-repository Apple install. That directory may not be writable by an ordinary account, which can matter for installation or updates even though running an already-installed router does not itself require admin privileges.
- **Router data:** The macOS `i2prouter` source selects `~/Library/Application Support/i2p` when that parent directory exists; otherwise it falls back to `~/.i2p`. The I2P+ FAQ independently lists `/Users/username/Library/Application Support/i2p` as the non-repository Apple settings folder.
- **Service configuration differs:** The legacy launchd plist is installed under `/Library/LaunchDaemons`, so its lifecycle is privileged and system-wide. Use the documented `i2prouter` commands for a user process; use launchd/service controls only if you deliberately installed that service.
- The FAQ and installation page describe the universal installer and paths, but the detailed lifecycle evidence is in the headless guide and the shipped scripts/templates. The live site’s current version and some GitHub/FAQ page content do not always align, so treat the repository source as the best evidence for script behavior.

## Sources read

- I2P+ install guide: https://github.com/vituperative/i2pplus/blob/master/docs/INSTALL.md
- I2P+ headless install/running/stopping guide: https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/blob/master/docs/INSTALL-headless.md
- I2P+ `i2prouter` source (macOS path detection and router management script): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/master/installer/resources/platform-specific/unix/i2prouter
- macOS service installer: https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/blob/master/installer/resources/platform-specific/macos/install_i2p_service_osx.command
- macOS service uninstaller: https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/blob/master/installer/resources/platform-specific/macos/uninstall_i2p_service_osx.command
- launchd plist template: https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/blob/master/installer/resources/platform-specific/macos/net.i2p.router.plist.template
- I2P+ FAQ (default Apple app/data paths): https://i2pplus.github.io/faq.html
- I2P+ installation page: https://i2pplus.github.io/installation.html"}]}

i2p_router_status() {

  router_script="$(i2p_router_script)"
  router_dir="$(dirname "$router_script")"
  printf 'I2P+ router command status:\n'
  (cd "$router_dir" && sh ./i2prouter status) || status_rc=$?
  status_rc="${status_rc:-0}"
  if i2p_proxy_ready; then
    printf 'Proxy endpoint: listening at 127.0.0.1:4444 (TCP only; bootstrap not verified)\n'
  else
    printf 'Proxy endpoint: not listening at 127.0.0.1:4444\n'
  fi
  return "$status_rc"
}

i2p_router_start() {
  local router_script router_dir
  router_script="$(i2p_router_script)"
  router_dir="$(dirname "$router_script")"
  if i2p_proxy_ready; then
    printf 'I2P+ proxy is already listening at 127.0.0.1:4444\n'
    return 0
  fi
  (cd "$router_dir" && sh ./i2prouter start) || fail "I2P+ router start command failed"
  printf 'I2P+ start requested. Synapse I2P browsing remains blocked until the proxy listens at 127.0.0.1:4444.\n'
}

i2p_router_stop() {
  local router_script router_dir
  router_script="$(i2p_router_script)"
  router_dir="$(dirname "$router_script")"
  (cd "$router_dir" && sh ./i2prouter graceful) || fail "I2P+ graceful shutdown command failed"
  printf 'I2P+ graceful shutdown requested.\n'
}

/does that call need to be added to the krypton framework?

No. The panel uses Krypton’s existing `exec()` from `k:proc_ex`; the current framework already has the call needed to invoke the macOS controller. See [the settings panel](src/control/i2p_settings.ks#L19) and [the macOS router commands](tools/synapse-macos.sh#L164).

For a production-quality integration, it would be better to add or use a framework API that launches a process with **separate arguments** and returns its exit status and output. The current `exec()` path goes through a shell and runs synchronously, which is acceptable for this prototype but is less robust and can make the UI wait. That’s a hardening improvement, not a prerequisite for the current feature.

{"kind":"reasoning","id":"p2-e130fdcb","text":"**Exploring API options**

I need to respond somehow about implying a hardening API might be necessary. I've found no process API in the project, which might require a framework change outside the project itself. The user seems okay with this suggestion, indicating permission to add an API to the Krypton framework. However, the developer's restrictions are preventing actions outside the project folder. I’m considering using Python as a local helper to avoid new dependencies. But the UI complicates things because of its synchronous nature. I think asynchronous adaptation is needed.**Evaluating shell exec options**

I think the current shell execution on macOS might support shell commands through the process API. I could modify runSettingsTool to use a command that captures output and status in the background. But I wonder if Krypton’s exec behavior waits for the child process to finish. The shell command's background operation should return immediately, but output might take time due to inherited stdout. 

Given that settings use sync exec, it might block the UI, although it could be acceptable. The user seems on board with building this based on their "ok" response, so I'll dig into the K framework repository path, but exploring external paths isn't an option.**Improving dynamic string safety**

I’m realizing that using a dynamic string for user-configured paths and arguments is generally safe. However, the current setup with `exec(... || true)` leads to losing the exit code and the ability to read text from the output. I think it’s better to change the shell interface to generate action outputs and status while avoiding the naive `|| true`. I want to ensure secure quoting by using functions and only allowing specific arguments.

It seems the `i2p-router-status` calls the path, but the process API expansion is outside my scope without the framework. I need to explain this more clearly to the user. I should find a way to proactively make this safer and consider if an asynchronous call via the shell would be beneficial. If the tool can run subprocesses with the process API, maybe I can create a helper command in the existing tools script to provide structured JSON outputs and errors.","open":false,"collapse":"preview"}

**It starts I2P+ as a background daemon, but it does not necessarily return immediately.** The current I2P+ startup script sets `WAIT_FOR_STARTED_STATUS=true`, invokes the wrapper in daemon mode, and then calls a startup-wait routine. That routine polls for the Java application’s `STARTED` status, with a configured timeout of **120 seconds**. On macOS, the script has a launchd-specific path when the launchd daemon is installed; it also calls the startup-wait routine.

Important distinction: **“STARTED” is not the same as the router being ready on the I2P network.** The wrapper’s status documentation defines Java `STARTED` as the application having reported to the wrapper that it is up. It does not establish that the router has integrated with the network or that tunnels/sites are usable.

There is also a fallback: the script’s polling loop can stop when status is `Unknown`; it then checks whether the process is still running. So the command can return without confirming `STARTED` if status reporting is unavailable. For a real readiness check, follow the startup with the local Router Console at `http://127.0.0.1:7657/` and check its connection state. Allow additional time for network integration.

**Sources:** [I2P+ startup script](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/master/installer/resources/platform-specific/unix/i2prouter) · [I2P+ install/run instructions](https://github.com/I2PPlus/i2pplus/blob/master/docs/INSTALL.md) · [Wrapper Java status definitions](https://wrapper.tanukisoftware.com/doc/english/prop-java-statusfile.html) · [Wrapper status definitions](https://wrapper.tanukisoftware.com/doc/english/prop-statusfile.html)

#!/bin/sh

# This runs the router by itself, WITHOUT the wrapper.
# This means the router will not restart if it crashes.
# Also, you will be using the default memory size, which is

# You should really use the i2prouter script instead.

# Paths
# Note that (percent)INSTALL_PATH and (percent)SYSTEM_java_io_tmpdir
# should have been replaced by the izpack installer.
# If you did not run the installer, replace them with the appropriate path.
I2P="/Applications/i2p"
I2PTEMP="/var/folders/k5/y23rgcf945j2rmd2nvyh6k2w0000gn/T/"

# next value to true may help.

CP=

# Uncomment to set the maximum memory. The default and the option may vary in different JVMs.
# Check your java documentation to be sure.
#MAXMEMOPT="-Xmx256m"

# Try using the Java binary that I2P was installed with.
# If it's not found, try looking in the system PATH.
JAVA=$(which "/Library/Internet Plug-Ins/JavaAppletPlugin.plugin/Contents/Home"/bin/java || which java)

if [ -z $JAVA ] || [ ! -x $JAVA ]; then
    echo "Error: Cannot find java." >&2
    exit 1
fi

for jar in `ls ${I2P}/lib/*.jar`; do
    if [ ! -z $CP ]; then
        CP=${CP}:${jar};
    else
        CP=${jar}
    fi
done

if [ $(uname -s) = "Darwin" ]; then
    export JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-Djava.awt.headless=true"
fi
JAVAOPTS="${MAXMEMOPT} -Djava.net.preferIPv4Stack=${PREFERv4} -Djava.library.path=${I2P}:${I2P}/lib -Di2p.dir.base=${I2P} -DloggerFilenameOverride=logs/log-router-@.txt"
(
    nohup ${JAVA} -cp \"${CP}\" ${JAVAOPTS} net.i2p.router.RouterLaunch > /dev/null 2>&1
) &
PID=$!

if [ ! -z $PID ] && kill -0 $PID > /dev/null 2>&1 ; then
    echo "I2P started [$PID]" >&2
    echo $PID > "${I2PTEMP}/router.pid"
else
    echo "I2P failed to start." >&2
    exit 1
fi

17-## Data directories

19-I2P+ stores configuration data in the user directory `~/.i2p/` on Linux

28-minimal copy that refers to the commented version. Do this before running
29-I2P+ for the first time.

33-| Platform            | Command                |

func applyOverlay() {
    if validateRoots("0") != "1" { emit "0" }
    let workspace = workspaceRoot()
    let root = firefoxRoot()
    let sourceBrowser = joinPath(joinPath(workspace, "overlay"), "browser")
    let destinationBrowser = joinPath(root, "browser")

    print("Applying Synapse browser overlay without deleting upstream files...")
    if copyOverlay(sourceBrowser, destinationBrowser) != "1" { emit "0" }
    if !exists(joinPath(joinPath(joinPath(joinPath(root, "browser"), "branding"), "synapse"), "configure.sh")) {
        print("Overlay verification failed: Synapse branding is missing.")
        emit "0"
    }
    if !exists(joinPath(joinPath(joinPath(joinPath(root, "browser"), "app"), "profile"), "synapse.js")) {
        print("Overlay verification failed: Synapse privacy preferences are missing.")
        emit "0"
    }
    if applyPrivacyPatch(workspace, root) != "1" { emit "0" }
    if installMozconfig(workspace, root) != "1" { emit "0" }
    print("Apply: complete")
    emit "1"
}

func printLogTail(logPath) {
    if !exists(logPath) {
        print("No mach log was created: " + logPath)
        emit "0"
    }
    let script = "Get-Content -LiteralPath '" + logPath + "' -Tail 80"
    let output = exec("powershell -NoProfile -Command " + quote(script))
    if len(output) > 0 { print(output) }
    emit "1"

{"kind":"tool","id":"g1gWjYjBDY8","toolName":"str_replace","input":{"path":"tools/synapse.ks","replacements":[{"oldString":"func applyPrivacyPatch(workspace, root) {
    let patchPath = joinPath(joinPath(joinPath(workspace, "overlay"), "privacy"), "privacy-loader.patch")

        emit "0"

    let check = "git -C " + quote(root) + " apply --check " + quote(patchPath)

        print("Privacy loader patch failed while applying.")
        emit "0"

    let reverse = "git -C " + quote(root) + " apply --reverse --check " + quote(patchPath)

    if contains(reverseOutput, "__SYNAPSE_OK__") {
        print("Synapse privacy loader patch is already applied.")
        emit "1"

    emit "0"
}
","newString":"func applyPatchIdempotently(root, patchPath, description) {
    if !exists(patchPath) {

    let check = "git -C " + quote(root) + " apply --check " + quote(patchPath)
    let checkOutput = exec(check + " >nul 2>&1 && echo __SYNAPSE_OK__ || echo __SYNAPSE_NO__")
    if contains(checkOutput, "__SYNAPSE_OK__") {
        let applyOutput = exec("git -C " + quote(root) + " apply " + quote(patchPath) + " 2>&1 && echo __SYNAPSE_OK__ || echo __SYNAPSE_FAIL__")
        if len(applyOutput) > 0 { print(applyOutput) }
        if contains(applyOutput, "__SYNAPSE_OK__") {
            print("Applied Synapse " + description + " patch.")
            emit "1"
        }
        print(description + " patch failed while applying.")
        emit "0"
    }

    let reverse = "git -C " + quote(root) + " apply --reverse --check " + quote(patchPath)
    let reverseOutput = exec(reverse + " >nul 2>&1 && echo __SYNAPSE_OK__ || echo __SYNAPSE_NO__")
    if contains(reverseOutput, "__SYNAPSE_OK__") {
        print("Synapse " + description + " patch is already applied.")
        emit "1"
    }

    print(description + " patch does not apply cleanly in either direction.")
    print("Source may have drifted; inspect: " + patchPath)
    emit "0"
}

func applyPrivacyPatch(workspace, root) {
    let patchPath = joinPath(joinPath(joinPath(workspace, "overlay"), "privacy"), "privacy-loader.patch")
    let themePatchPath = joinPath(joinPath(joinPath(workspace, "overlay"), "privacy"), "synapse-theme.patch")
    if applyPatchIdempotently(root, patchPath, "privacy loader") != "1" { emit "0" }
    if applyPatchIdempotently(root, themePatchPath, "browser theme") != "1" { emit "0" }
    emit "1"
}

Yes — the architecture we already built for I2P generalizes cleanly to a Tor profile, and the roadmap already reserves it (M3: "Integrate Tor with fail-closed routing tests"). Here's the honest assessment:

**What works immediately (1–2 days of work, macOS):**
- A dedicated `synapse-tor-<identity>` profile following the exact I2P pattern: generated `user.js`, isolated from your normal browsing profile, launched with its own window via `tor-open` (parallel to `i2p-open`).
- The proxy gate flips from I2P's HTTP proxy (4444) to Tor's SOCKS5 (9050) with `network.proxy.socks`, `socksRemoteDNS` (DNS resolved inside Tor), `no_proxies_on` localhost, DIRECT fallback and prefetch/WebRTC/HTTP3 disabled — Firefox core already handles `.onion` routing through the SOCKS proxy.
- The same fail-closed contract as I2P: browser stays locked until the Tor SOCKS listener actually answers, plus "Tor is bootstrapping / not ready" states instead of errors that look like the phishing warning.
- The Router Console start page becomes a Tor status page (or the Tor control-auth check page).

**What's genuinely different from I2P:**
- **Circuit isolation depth.** Tor Browser isolates browsing state per-container via the Tor control port (first-party isolation) and nukes history/session between uses. Without the control port, two tabs in the same Tor profile share a circuit in the browser's eyes and can be linked. Doing this properly means talking to Tor's control port from Krypton (or ChromeNative messaging) — that's the same "authenticate and attest listener ownership" work item I2P already has pending.
- **Bundling the daemon.** Same question you asked about I2P+ — bundling Tor is allowed (Tor Browser does it) but you need the update/signing story; using a user-installed Tor is the simpler v1.
- **Leak testing.** Fingerprinting/egress tests for Tor have higher stakes and the roadmap has a dedicated M3 item for them, including an independent security assessment before any "certification" claim.

**So: Shield (hardened default), I2P, Tor coexist fine** because they're three separate profile contexts spawning separate windows — no conflict — as long as only one proxy mode is active per profile (which our dedicated-profile design guarantees).

I'd sequence it: Tor profile + launcher + fail-closed gate + status page first (well-understood, testable today), then Tor control-port circuit isolation as the trust-hardening pass, reusing the I2P listener-attestation work so both modes solve it once.

/* Synapse browser chrome palette, tuned to the Krypton brand scheme
 * (krypton-lang.org, kryptonbytes.com) and adaptive to the system
 * appearance: Light/Golden Gate gets the site's light scheme, Dark gets
 * its near-black indigo scheme. The macOS menu bar follows the window's
 * used color scheme, so declaring nothing here keeps it consistent once
 * more. Forced-colors and high-contrast modes stay authoritative. */
@media not ((forced-colors) or (-moz-native-theme)) {
  :root:not([lwtheme]) {
    /* Surfaces: light from krypton-lang.org (:root light theme), dark from
     * kryptonbytes.com (--nav-bg, --bg, --code-bg, cards). */
    --toolbox-background-color: light-dark(#fafafa, #0a0a0f);
    --toolbox-background-color-inactive: light-dark(#f2f2f6, #0e0e15);
    --toolbox-text-color: light-dark(#222222, #f5f5fb);
    --toolbox-text-color-inactive: light-dark(#555555, #9a9ab2);
    --toolbar-background-color: light-dark(#ffffff, #0f0f17);
    --toolbar-text-color: light-dark(#222222, #f5f5fb);
    --toolbar-field-background-color: light-dark(#f0edff, #0b0b15);
    --toolbar-field-text-color: light-dark(#222222, #f5f5fb);
    --toolbar-field-border-color: light-dark(#e0e0e0, #2a2a3c);
    --toolbar-field-background-color-focus: light-dark(#ffffff, #0b0b15);
    --toolbar-field-text-color-focus: light-dark(#222222, #f5f5fb);
    --toolbar-field-border-color-focus: light-dark(#7722ff, #7722ff);
    --background-color-box: light-dark(#ffffff, #1a1a26);

    /* Signals: Krypton violet on both sides. */
    --toolbarbutton-icon-fill: light-dark(#555555, #e8ddff);
    --toolbarbutton-icon-fill-attention: light-dark(#7722ff, #a974ff);
    --tab-background-color-selected: light-dark(#f0edff, #1a1a26);
    --tab-text-color-selected: light-dark(#222222, #f5f5fb);
    --link-color: light-dark(#7722ff, #a974ff);
    --link-color-hover: light-dark(#5d16da, #c0a0ff);
    --link-color-active: light-dark(#3a0ca3, #7722ff);

    /* Structure: the site borders, violet-tinted dark separators. */
    --tabs-navbar-separator-color: light-dark(rgb(0 0 0 / 10%), rgb(119 34 255 / 35%));
    --chrome-content-separator-color: light-dark(rgb(0 0 0 / 8%), rgb(119 34 255 / 28%));
    --focus-outline-color: #7722ff;
    --color-accent-attention: light-dark(#7722ff, #8842ff);

    /* Interaction layer: violet-tinted hovers over each mode's surface.
     * Values live here until the M4 token pass names them. */
    --toolbarbutton-background-color-hover:
      light-dark(rgb(0 0 0 / 6%), rgb(119 34 255 / 18%));
    --toolbarbutton-background-color-active:
      light-dark(rgb(0 0 0 / 10%), rgb(119 34 255 / 30%));
    --button-background-color-hover: light-dark(rgb(0 0 0 / 5%), rgb(255 255 255 / 9%));
    --button-background-color-active: light-dark(rgb(0 0 0 / 9%), rgb(255 255 255 / 16%));

    /* Panels (all-tabs popup, identity panel, app panels): Krypton surfaces
     * per mode so menu items are always legible. */
    --panel-background-color: light-dark(#ffffff, #1a1a26);
    --panel-border-color: light-dark(#e0e0e0, #2a2a3c);
    --panel-text-color: light-dark(#222222, #f5f5fb);

    /* macOS: the titlebar strip must draw with the chrome palette instead
     * of the system titlebar material, which otherwise tints light gray
     * through the dark toolbox. Explicit backgrounds for the titlebar rows. */
    @media (-moz-platform: macos) {
      :root:not([lwtheme]):not([macOSNativeFullscreen])[customtitlebar] body::after {
        appearance: none !important;
        background-color: var(--toolbox-background-color) !important;
      }

      .browser-titlebar {
        background-color: var(--toolbox-background-color) !important;
      }
    }
  }
}

// Synapse start page address bar label.
//
// When the selected tab is showing the Synapse start page
// (the Synapse start page URL, browser.newtab.url), the address bar
// shows a friendly "Start Page" label instead of the URL.  The label is
// presentation-only: focusing the bar restores the real URL so it
// remains fully editable, and the identity box (padlock), page proxy

{
  let LABEL = "Start Page";
  let PREF = "browser.newtab.url";
  let gSynapseStartPageOverridden = false;

  let startPageSpec = () => {
    let startPage = Services.prefs
      .getStringPref(PREF, "about:newtab")
      .trim();
    if (!startPage || startPage === "about:newtab") {
      // No Synapse start page configured; show real URLs as usual.
      return null;
    }

    // Normalize so a trailing slash in the pref doesn't break matching.
    try {
      return Services.io.newURI(startPage).spec.replace(/\/$/, "");
    } catch (e) {
      return null;
    }
  };

  let currentSpec = () => {
    let browser = gBrowser?.selectedBrowser;
    let uri = browser?.currentURI;
    if (!uri) {
      return null;
    }
    try {
      return Services.io.newURI(uri.spec).spec.replace(/\/$/, "");
    } catch (e) {
      return null;
    }
  };

  let updateURLBar = () => {
    if (!gURLBar || !gBrowser) {
      return;
    }

    let isStartPage = !!startPageSpec() && startPageSpec() === currentSpec();
    if (isStartPage && !gURLBar.focused) {
      gSynapseStartPageOverridden = true;
      gURLBar.value = LABEL;
      // Setting .value marks the bar as edited and shows the clear
      // button; restoring proxy state keeps the identity glyph/lock and
      // ensures the URL is treated as unmodified chrome state.
      gURLBar.setPageProxyState("valid", false);
    } else if (gSynapseStartPageOverridden) {
      clearURLBar();
    }
  };

  let clearURLBar = () => {
    if (!gURLBar || !gSynapseStartPageOverridden) {
      return;
    }
    gSynapseStartPageOverridden = false;
    let uri = gBrowser?.selectedBrowser?.currentURI;
    if (uri) {
      gURLBar.setURI({ uri, isSameDocument: true });
    }
  };

  let init = () => {
    if (!gURLBar || !gBrowser) {
      return;
    }

    // The real URL is restored while the bar is focused (so the user
    // can edit / select it) and reapplied on blur.
    gURLBar.addEventListener("focus", clearURLBar);
    gURLBar.addEventListener("blur", updateURLBar);

    // Location changes (including simulated ones when switching tabs)
    // determine whether the label should be shown.
    gBrowser.addTabsProgressListener({
      onLocationChange(aBrowser, aWebProgress, aRequest, aLocationURI) {
        updateURLBar();
      },

    // so the label never leaks into session-restore or crash-restore
    // paths that read the visible URL bar contents.
    let onTabRestored = () => {
      if (gURLBar.focused) {
        // The URL bar keeps focus across tab switches - restore the
        // new tab's real URL before deciding on a new label.
        gSynapseStartPageOverridden = false;
      }
      updateURLBar();
    };
    gBrowser.tabContainer.addEventListener("TabSelect", onTabRestored);
    gBrowser.tabContainer.addEventListener("TabMove", onTabRestored);
    gBrowser.tabContainer.addEventListener("TabClose", onTabRestored);

    window.addEventListener("beforeunload", clearURLBar);

    updateURLBar();
  };

  // which has completed by the time the window load event fires.
  window.addEventListener("load", () => init(), { once: true });
}

**Root cause:** the first-tab stall was a **default-pref collision**. Two files ship defaults — `firefox.js` (stock) and `synapse.js` (ours) — and both defined `browser.startup.homepage` / `browser.startup.page`. The load order between default pref files in the same directory isn't guaranteed, and Firefox's stock `about:home` was winning over our start-page URL. That's why the diagnostics showed the first tab receiving `about:home` as its startup URI and never loading (it stalled in the about-redirect pipeline), while second tabs — which go through `about:newtab` and a pref only synapse.js defines (`browser.newtab.url`) — worked fine.

Both edge paths are fixed and verified now.

**What was wrong with your run:** when the first tab's startup URI resolved to `about:home` (through the stock homepage default path), the redirector rewrote it to the start page *at the channel level*, but Gecko's docshell never commits that channel for the startup tab — the document stayed `about:blank` forever. The "Start Page" label still showed because the label code counts `about:home` as the start page, but behind it there was no page. I reproduced exactly that with a test profile.

**The fix:** instead of relying on that channel-level redirect for startup, Synapse now substitutes the start-page URL directly into the window's startup arguments — the same technique Gecko already uses for its own start screen. So the first tab always receives `https://www.krypton-lang.org/s.html` as a plain web URL and loads it normally.

**Verified with fresh-profile runs against the rebuilt app:**

- Homepage = `about:home` (the failing case): first tab loads the start page, doc commits, "Start Page" label asserted
- Default profile (no user prefs): identical result — load + label, no regression
- Rebuilt and reinstalled to [/Applications/Synapse.app](/Applications/Synapse.app) again, so what's installed now is the fixed build

Note this covers first-launch behavior; it still can't affect pages you've pre-navigated with your own user-pref homepage, which keep winning as designed.
